facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The reported base is clear and current to September 30, 2026. Element Solutions carries total debt of 3.09x LTM Adjusted EBITDA at Q3 2026, but 2026 changed its structure: it bought EFC for cash on hand and Micromax with new term loans, so debt rose by 456.2 and cash fell by 401.6 between December 31, 2025 and September 30, 2026. LTM leverage is therefore overstated relative to a full-year run rate of the acquired businesses, which contribute only from January 2 and February 2, 2026. Separately, Adjusted EBITDA adds back acquisition, integration and transaction costs of 52.6 for nine months 2026, so the ratio flatters cash earnings. Reported net sales growth of 52% in Q3 2026 includes acquisitions and higher pass-through metals prices; organic growth was 13%. Cash generation is thinner than EBITDA growth suggests: nine-month operating cash flow of 192.2 is below the 198.7 of nine months 2025 despite higher Adjusted EBITDA, because receivables and inventories absorbed cash. The 800.0 of senior notes in 2028 and 1,279.7 of term loans in 2030 are the only large maturities, and the revolver was 15.0 drawn at September 30, 2026. Every ratio below is the analyst's calculation on a labelled basis; none is a covenant ratio.

facts.label: Narrative review
facts.text: - Leverage: total debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA was 3.09x at Q3 2026, down from 3.71x at Q1 2026 and 3.37x at Q2 2026 but above 2.97x at FY2025. Mechanism: the add-on term loans of 449.4 (net of discount) and a revolver draw funded Micromax while EFC was paid from cash on hand, so debt rose and cash fell while LTM EBITDA includes the acquired businesses only partly. Implication: from Q1 2026 to Q3 2026 the ratio fell mainly because LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 581.5 to 673.1, helped by net revolver repayment of 70.0 across Q2 and Q3 2026 (R3 p8: "Changes in lines of credit, net (35.0) (35.0) 85.0"); term loan repayments were only 6.4 in nine months 2026. - Coverage: Adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest paid 7.85x on the LTM basis, slightly below 7.98x at FY2025, as interest paid rose to 85.7 LTM. Accrual interest expense, net, rose 68.6% in nine months 2026 against nine months 2025. Interest cost is partly fixed through swaps (about 94% of debt fixed per the release), so a rise in SOFR has limited effect, but the euro-denominated swap legs add foreign exchange sensitivity. - Cash flow quality: nine-month operating cash flow of 192.2 was 35.8% of Adjusted EBITDA of 536.8, against 48.3% in nine months 2025, because rising metals prices tied up working capital (receivables outflow 137.3, inventories 80.7). Q3 2026 alone was 159.2, after 99.6 in Q2 2026 and an outflow of 66.6 in Q1 2026. The 10-Q attributes the nine-month shortfall to "higher investment in working capital from rising metals prices" (Q3-26 p45). Implication: cash conversion is seasonal and metals-price dependent; it rebounded in Q3 2026. - Liquidity: 702.9 of cash plus undrawn revolver against a first large maturity of 800.0 on September 1, 2028. Cash of 224.9 is mostly (176) held by foreign subsidiaries, so it is not all available to the U.S. borrowers without transfer cost. - Earnings trend: Adjusted EBITDA rose each quarter in 2026 (162.3, 183.5, 191.0) and management raised 2026 guidance to approximately 720 (R3 p2, guidance, not a reported figure). Specialties Adjusted EBITDA fell year on year in Q3 2026. - Data quality: the quarterly columns add to the nine-month columns; the Adjusted EBITDA reconciliations add exactly; carrying and face debt reconcile to the stated discounts and costs (C8, C10). - Definition risks: issuer Adjusted EBITDA adds back acquisition, integration and transaction costs (52.6 for nine months 2026, 34.9 for FY2025), FY2025 executive share grants (37.1), restructuring and other items, and excludes unrealized metals derivative results. The Q3 2026 acquisition cost line may include costs of the terminated Solstice merger; the split is not supplied. Covenant EBITDA is defined in the Credit Agreement, not supplied. - Key gaps: Credit Agreement and indenture; Termination Agreement; pro forma EBITDA for the acquisitions; covenant ratio; operating lease update after December 31, 2025.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: Element Solutions is a Delaware specialty chemicals technology company with two segments: Electronics (MacDermid Alpha Electronics Solutions) and Specialties (Element Specialties). Its products are consumed in customers' production processes, which gives recurring replenishment demand, and no customer reaches 10% of net sales. The credit-relevant change in 2026 is structural. EFC (closed January 2, 2026) was paid for from cash on hand and Micromax (closed February 2, 2026) from $450 million of add-on term loans and revolver borrowings, so the business is larger, more Electronics-weighted and more exposed to precious-metal pass-through pricing than at FY2025. A proposed acquisition of the company by Solstice Advanced Materials Inc. was signed on July 6, 2026 and terminated on August 27, 2026 with a mutual release; the supplied filings do not say whether any termination fee or cost arose. The company is publicly listed and no sponsor is identified in the sources read, and the documented governance behaviour is mixed rather than adverse: a debt-funded acquisition year, continued dividends and buybacks, and a modest related-party advisory fee. The main creditor uncertainties are the integration and valuation of the acquisitions, metal-price-driven working capital, and the unsupplied terms of the terminated merger.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: Solstice merger. On July 6, 2026 the company entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger with Solstice Advanced Materials Inc., Solar Merger Sub One Inc. and Solar Merger Sub Two LLC (Q3-26 p3: "dated as of July 6, 2026"). Under the terms disclosed in the Q2 10-Q, each share of common stock would convert into "0.5 shares of Solstice common stock" and "$10.00 in cash", with closing "expected to close in the first half of 2027" and conditions that included stockholder approval of both companies, an effective Form S-4, listing approval and expiry of the Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period (Q2-26 p12). The Q2 10-Q disclosed that if the Merger Agreement were terminated "in certain circumstances, we could be required to pay to Solstice a termination fee of $376,000,000" and that the company might "use available cash, including by drawdown on our revolving credit facility" to do so (Q2-26 p50). On August 27, 2026 the parties entered into a Termination Agreement; the Q3 10-Q states the parties "mutually agreed to terminate the Merger Agreement which, subject to customary exceptions, mutually released the parties from any claims of liability" (Q3-26 p12). The Q3 10-Q does not state that any termination fee was paid or accrued and does not state the cost of the transaction; the Termination Agreement is listed as an exhibit to a Form 8-K filed on August 27, 2026 (Q3-26 p49) that is not in the pack. Management Language: the chief executive described the company's "standalone, independent trajectory" as having "only improved" (R3 p2). Insufficient Information: whether a termination fee or other cost arose, the cost of the terminated process within "Acquisition, integration and transaction expenses" of 21.9 in Q3 2026 (Q3-26 p27), and the reason for termination are not in the supplied sources. Liquidity effect: the Q2 10-Q summary does not describe how the company's debt would have been treated at closing (Insufficient Information); with the merger terminated, the existing Credit Agreement and 3.875% USD Notes due 2028 remain the capital structure (CP-1).

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: - Revenue durability. Evidence: recurring consumable products, no customer at 10% of net sales and minimal backlog (K25 p8, p16). Mechanic: broad customer base lowers single-name loss risk, while minimal backlog means revenue follows customers' production in short cycles. Implication: debt service is supported by diversification, but earnings can fall quickly in an electronics downturn; the Q3 2026 organic growth of 13% (CP-1) is demand driven and could reverse. - Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: pass-through metals were 40.9% of Q3 2026 Electronics sales against 26.9% a year earlier (A3) and the gross margin fell to 34.4% from 42.2% (A4). Mechanic: higher metal prices lift revenue and working capital without lifting profit proportionally and tie up cash in receivables and inventories (Q3-26 p45). Implication: reported revenue growth overstates operating growth, and cash conversion weakens when metals rise, as in nine months 2026 where operating cash flow fell while Adjusted EBITDA rose (CP-1). - Concentration risk. Evidence: Electronics is 78.3% of Q3 2026 net sales and 77.6% of segment Adjusted EBITDA (A1); China is 21.9% of FY2025 net sales (A2). Mechanic: demand in AI infrastructure and high-performance electronics drives Electronics (R3 p2, Management Language), and China exposure adds trade-policy sensitivity named in the filing's forward-looking factors (Q3-26 p4). Implication: segment and country concentration raise cyclical and trade exposure; Specialties, which fell in Q3 2026, is a smaller offset. - Owner and governance alignment. Evidence: no sponsor, a terminated sale, acquisition-led leverage and continued shareholder returns. Mechanic: a public company with discretionary buybacks can lever up for acquisitions or return cash; the Credit Agreement's springing test does not bind at the current revolver draw (CP-1). Implication: creditor protection depends on documents that are not supplied; behaviour to date is mixed, not adverse. The logged conflict on the acquisition prices does not alter this reading. - Acquisition integration. Evidence: preliminary allocations, goodwill of 292.7 added (Q3-26 p14: "Acquisitions (2) 128.9 163.8 292.7"), and acquisition, integration and transaction expenses of 52.6 for nine months 2026 (CP-1). Mechanic: add-backs and fair value changes make acquired earnings harder to verify. Implication: leverage on LTM EBITDA should be monitored against a pro forma figure, which is not supplied. - Key uncertainties: terms and any cost of the terminated merger, covenant and indenture definitions, post-October 22, 2026 events, ratings.

citations.quote: Thesis: Element Solutions can service its debt from growing earnings with adequate liquidity and a distant first maturity, but 2026 acquisitions lifted leverage, cash conversion is thinner than earnings, and unverified add-backs and covenant terms limit how much comfort the reported ratios give.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: 1. Leverage rose with the 2026 acquisitions. Total debt rose to USD 2,082.1 million at September 30, 2026 from USD 1,625.9 million at December 31, 2025, while cash fell to USD 224.9 million from USD 626.5 million, so net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA is 2.76x against 1.83x at FY2025 (CP-1 C4). Mechanism: EFC was paid from cash and Micromax from USD 450 million of add-on term loans plus revolver borrowings (CP-1A transaction summary), so gross debt rose while the acquired earnings enter LTM only from January 2 and February 2, 2026. Implication: LTM leverage overstates a full-year run rate and is falling as earnings arrive (3.71x at Q1 2026 to 3.09x), but the starting point is higher and the cushion for further debt-funded deals is smaller. Documentary Fact via CP-1; Analyst Interpretation on direction. 2. Coverage is strong. Adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest paid 7.85x and net interest expense 8.29x on the LTM basis (CP-1 C5), slightly below 7.98x on cash interest at FY2025. Mechanism: about 94% of debt is fixed through swaps and the 3.875% USD Notes due 2028, so higher floating rates have limited effect, although the euro-denominated swap legs add currency sensitivity (CP-1 debt register). Implication: low near-term debt service strain unless earnings fall sharply. Documentary Fact via CP-1. 3. Earnings are growing, but part of the growth is acquired or metals-driven. Nine-month 2026 Adjusted EBITDA of USD 536.8 million is above USD 411.3 million a year earlier (CP-1 C13), and quarterly Adjusted EBITDA rose each quarter of 2026. Reported Q3 2026 net sales growth of 52% compares with organic growth of 13% (CP-1), because acquisitions and pass-through metals pricing lifted reported sales (CP-1A operating rows). Mechanism: higher metal prices raise revenue and working capital without proportional profit, and gross margin fell to 34.4% from 42.2% (CP-1A A4). Implication: reported growth overstates underlying growth, and margin should be assessed on an ex-metals basis. Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on quality. 4. Cash conversion lags earnings. Nine-month operating cash flow of USD 192.2 million was 35.8% of Adjusted EBITDA, against 48.3% in the same period of 2025, and below USD 198.7 million a year earlier despite higher earnings (CP-1 C13). Mechanism: receivables and inventories absorbed cash as metal prices rose; Q3 2026 alone produced USD 159.2 million after an outflow of USD 66.6 million in Q1 2026. Implication: free cash flow of USD 182.9 million LTM (CP-1 C6) is thinner than EBITDA suggests and is seasonal and metals-price dependent. Documentary Fact via CP-1. 5. Liquidity is adequate and the first maturity is distant, but larger than liquidity. Cash plus undrawn revolver is USD 702.9 million, of which USD 176 million of cash is held by foreign subsidiaries (CP-1 C7, narrative review). The USD 800.0 million of notes due September 1, 2028 exceed liquidity by USD 97.1 million (CP-1 C13), and term loans of USD 1,279.7 million mature on December 18, 2030. Implication: repayment depends on cash generation or refinancing, with about 22 months to act as at the as-of date; the first maturity is a monitoring point rather than a near-term constraint. Documentary Fact via CP-1. 6. The terminated Solstice merger leaves unanswered questions. A merger signed on July 6, 2026 was terminated on August 27, 2026 with a mutual release, and the Q2 10-Q disclosed a possible USD 376,000,000 termination fee in certain circumstances (CP-1A transaction summary). Whether any fee or cost arose is not stated, and the add-back for acquisition, integration and transaction expenses of USD 52.6 million for nine months 2026 may include process costs (CP-1). Implication: a potential cash cost is unquantified, and the change-of-control risk that would have applied is removed. Documentary Fact for the termination; Insufficient Information for any payment. 7. Shareholder returns and add-backs temper the quality of earnings. Dividends of USD 59.3 million and buybacks of USD 37.7 million in nine months 2026 total USD 97.0 million, with approximately USD 518 million of authorisation remaining (CP-1, CP-1A governance rows); Adjusted EBITDA adds back USD 37.1 million of 2025 executive share grants and USD 52.6 million of acquisition-related costs (CP-1 narrative review). Mechanism: discretionary distributions compete with debt reduction, and add-backs lift the earnings base that leverage ratios use. Implication: leverage tolerance should be read on cash earnings after these items; creditor limits on distributions are not supplied. Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation. 8. Covenant protection is thin on the facts supplied. The only financial covenant located is a springing first lien net leverage test of 5.0 to 1.0, applying when revolver borrowings exceed 30% of the USD 500.0 million commitment; USD 15.0 million is drawn (CP-1). The indicative first lien net leverage is 1.59x and USD 135.0 million of further drawing is possible before the test applies (CP-1 C12), but these are not covenant ratios. Implication: the facility offers little ongoing maintenance discipline while the revolver is lightly used, and headroom cannot be monitored without the Credit Agreement definitions. Documentary Fact; headroom Not calculable.

## Request
- Issuer: Element Solutions Inc (issuer id `esi`, NYSE: ESI), as of 2026-11-05, information cutoff 2026-11-05 (context). Reporting currency USD; current period Q3 2026; prior period FY2025 (context).
- Run: `esi-2026-11-05-credit_snapshot-host`, pathway `credit_snapshot`, requested modules CP-1, CP-1A, CP-2 and CP-5 (the launcher's `minimum` set). CP-0 runs first as their dependency.
- Execution: host session. The host searched and opened the pinned page files and wrote this answer. No provider was called.
- Question: can the supplied public filings and earnings releases support CP-1, CP-1A, CP-2 and CP-5, and what remains blocked?

- Assertion: SOURCE_SUFFICIENCY_ONLY; CP_MODEL_INPUT_CONTRACT_NOT_EVALUATED. No credit conclusion, legal interpretation or investment opinion is given; no figure is normalized, reconciled or calculated here.

- Scope of reading: the sources are page-chunked text (`page:N`); locators below are those chunks, not printed page numbers. This module opened the cover, statements, debt, liquidity, covenant, segment, transaction and subsequent-event pages of each source. Pages it did not open (for example most risk-factor, tax, pension and environmental pages of the annual report) are retained evidence that this module did not assess, not excluded evidence.

### Readiness view

The effective source set is sufficient to start all four requested analyses, and each is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS rather than READY. The limitations are missing governing documents and a gap after the last filing, not missing financial statements. Filed statements and notes control their respective facts; the earnings releases are attributed management presentations and are used only for what the filings do not print. None of the sources has blocked preparation, and none is a duplicate of another. This is source sufficiency only; it does not evaluate the downstream model input contract, and it does not state whether any downstream analysis is complete.

### Financial base view

The reported base is clear and current to September 30, 2026. Element Solutions carries total debt of 3.09x LTM Adjusted EBITDA at Q3 2026, but 2026 changed its structure: it bought EFC for cash on hand and Micromax with new term loans, so debt rose by 456.2 and cash fell by 401.6 between December 31, 2025 and September 30, 2026. LTM leverage is therefore overstated relative to a full-year run rate of the acquired businesses, which contribute only from January 2 and February 2, 2026. Separately, Adjusted EBITDA adds back acquisition, integration and transaction costs of 52.6 for nine months 2026, so the ratio flatters cash earnings. Reported net sales growth of 52% in Q3 2026 includes acquisitions and higher pass-through metals prices; organic growth was 13%. Cash generation is thinner than EBITDA growth suggests: nine-month operating cash flow of 192.2 is below the 198.7 of nine months 2025 despite higher Adjusted EBITDA, because receivables and inventories absorbed cash. The 800.0 of senior notes in 2028 and 1,279.7 of term loans in 2030 are the only large maturities, and the revolver was 15.0 drawn at September 30, 2026. - Definition risks: issuer Adjusted EBITDA adds back acquisition, integration and transaction costs (52.6 for nine months 2026, 34.9 for FY2025), FY2025 executive share grants (37.1), restructuring and other items, and excludes unrealized metals derivative results. The Q3 2026 acquisition cost line may include costs of the terminated Solstice merger; the split is not supplied. Covenant EBITDA is defined in the Credit Agreement, not supplied.

### Business and transaction view

Element Solutions is a Delaware specialty chemicals technology company with two segments: Electronics (MacDermid Alpha Electronics Solutions) and Specialties (Element Specialties). Its products are consumed in customers' production processes, which gives recurring replenishment demand, and no customer reaches 10% of net sales. The credit-relevant change in 2026 is structural. EFC (closed January 2, 2026) was paid for from cash on hand and Micromax (closed February 2, 2026) from $450 million of add-on term loans and revolver borrowings, so the business is larger, more Electronics-weighted and more exposed to precious-metal pass-through pricing than at FY2025. A proposed acquisition of the company by Solstice Advanced Materials Inc. was signed on July 6, 2026 and terminated on August 27, 2026 with a mutual release; the supplied filings do not say whether any termination fee or cost arose. The company is publicly listed and no sponsor is identified in the sources read, and the documented governance behaviour is mixed rather than adverse: a debt-funded acquisition year, continued dividends and buybacks, and a modest related-party advisory fee. The main creditor uncertainties are the integration and valuation of the acquisitions, metal-price-driven working capital, and the unsupplied terms of the terminated merger.
| Driver | View | Category |
| Transaction and ownership | Merger signed then terminated; public company, no sponsor | Documentary Fact |
| Business and operating model | Two segments, recurring consumable products, no customer at 10% of net sales, metals pass-through | Documentary Fact |

Solstice merger. On July 6, 2026 the company entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger with Solstice Advanced Materials Inc., Solar Merger Sub One Inc. and Solar Merger Sub Two LLC (Q3-26 p3: "dated as of July 6, 2026"). Under the terms disclosed in the Q2 10-Q, each share of common stock would convert into "0.5 shares of Solstice common stock" and "$10.00 in cash", with closing "expected to close in the first half of 2027" and conditions that included stockholder approval of both companies, an effective Form S-4, listing approval and expiry of the Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period (Q2-26 p12). The Q2 10-Q disclosed that if the Merger Agreement were terminated "in certain circumstances, we could be required to pay to Solstice a termination fee of $376,000,000" and that the company might "use available cash, including by drawdown on our revolving credit facility" to do so (Q2-26 p50). On August 27, 2026 the parties entered into a Termination Agreement; the Q3 10-Q states the parties "mutually agreed to terminate the Merger Agreement which, subject to customary exceptions, mutually released the parties from any claims of liability" (Q3-26 p12). EFC and Micromax. EFC Gases & Advanced Materials was acquired on January 2, 2026 "for a purchase price of approximately $367 million, net of cash and subject to adjustments", plus a potential earn-out of "up to $30.0 million cash or 1.16 million shares", funded with cash on hand (Q3-26 p12). Micromax (US) Holdings LLC was acquired on February 2, 2026 "for a purchase price of approximately $494 million, net of cash and subject to adjustments", funded with the Add-on Term Loans of $450 million and revolver borrowings (Q3-26 p12). The 10-K's subsequent-events note estimated the prices at approximately $369 million and $500 million (K25 p126), logged as a conflict below; the later filing controls. Cash paid for acquisitions was 865.8 for nine months 2026 (CP-1). Goodwill of 128.9 for Micromax and 163.8 for EFC was recorded and the purchase price allocations are "preliminary" (Q3-26 p13, p14). The acquisitions were "not significant" so pro forma results were not presented (Q3-26 p14), which means no pro forma EBITDA is available (Insufficient Information; CP-1 gaps).

New debt issues and financing. No new bond was issued in 2026 in the supplied filings. On February 2, 2026 the company syndicated $450 million of Add-on Term Loans with "identical terms as the then existing term loans B-3, including a maturity date of December 18, 2030", and a "5-year $500 million senior secured revolving credit facility, which replaced its then existing $375 million revolving credit facility" with maturity extended to 2031 (Q3-26 p16). The term loans bear SOFR plus 1.75% and the revolver SOFR plus 1.50% (Q3-26 p15). Swaps convert "$350 million of the Add-on Term Loans" into fixed euro-denominated debt through December 2029 (Q3-26 p20). Revolver borrowings fell from 85.0 at Q1 2026 to 15.0 at Q3 2026. ### Credit translations

- Revenue durability. Evidence: recurring consumable products, no customer at 10% of net sales and minimal backlog (K25 p8, p16). Mechanic: broad customer base lowers single-name loss risk, while minimal backlog means revenue follows customers' production in short cycles. Implication: debt service is supported by diversification, but earnings can fall quickly in an electronics downturn; the Q3 2026 organic growth of 13% (CP-1) is demand driven and could reverse.

- Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: pass-through metals were 40.9% of Q3 2026 Electronics sales against 26.9% a year earlier (A3) and the gross margin fell to 34.4% from 42.2% (A4). Mechanic: higher metal prices lift revenue and working capital without lifting profit proportionally and tie up cash in receivables and inventories (Q3-26 p45). Implication: reported revenue growth overstates operating growth, and cash conversion weakens when metals rise, as in nine months 2026 where operating cash flow fell while Adjusted EBITDA rose (CP-1).

- Concentration risk. Evidence: Electronics is 78.3% of Q3 2026 net sales and 77.6% of segment Adjusted EBITDA (A1); China is 21.9% of FY2025 net sales (A2). Mechanic: demand in AI infrastructure and high-performance electronics drives Electronics (R3 p2, Management Language), and China exposure adds trade-policy sensitivity named in the filing's forward-looking factors (Q3-26 p4). Implication: segment and country concentration raise cyclical and trade exposure; Specialties, which fell in Q3 2026, is a smaller offset.

- Owner and governance alignment. Evidence: no sponsor, a terminated sale, acquisition-led leverage and continued shareholder returns. Mechanic: a public company with discretionary buybacks can lever up for acquisitions or return cash; the Credit Agreement's springing test does not bind at the current revolver draw (CP-1). Implication: creditor protection depends on documents that are not supplied; behaviour to date is mixed, not adverse. The logged conflict on the acquisition prices does not alter this reading.

- Acquisition integration. Evidence: preliminary allocations, goodwill of 292.7 added (Q3-26 p14: "Acquisitions (2) 128.9 163.8 292.7"), and acquisition, integration and transaction expenses of 52.6 for nine months 2026 (CP-1). Mechanic: add-backs and fair value changes make acquired earnings harder to verify. Implication: leverage on LTM EBITDA should be monitored against a pro forma figure, which is not supplied.
- Key uncertainties: terms and any cost of the terminated merger, covenant and indenture definitions, post-October 22, 2026 events, ratings.

- Scope: the fundamental credit view, with the strengths, weaknesses, findings, risks and gaps that drive it, built only from the CP-0, CP-1 and CP-1A handoffs; it fills "Key findings" and "Strengths and weaknesses".

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Element Solutions has moderate reported leverage of 3.09x, strong earnings growth, cash interest cover of 7.85x and adequate liquidity of USD 702.9 million. Debt-funded acquisitions raised leverage, and cash conversion is weaker than earnings. | Medium | Covenant definitions, the terminated merger's terms and pro forma EBITDA for the acquisitions are not supplied. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Total debt rose to USD 2,082.1 million from USD 1,625.9 million after two acquisitions, lifting net leverage to 2.76x from 1.83x. | Leverage is above FY2025 but falling as earnings arrive, from 3.71x total at Q1 2026, leaving less room for further debt-funded deals. | High |

| Adjusted EBITDA reached USD 673.1 million over the last twelve months, but cash conversion fell as metals prices tied up working capital. | Earnings growth supports debt service only if cash flow follows; free cash flow was USD 182.9 million. | Medium |

| The first large maturity is USD 800.0 million of senior notes due September 1, 2028, above liquidity of USD 702.9 million. | Repayment relies on cash generation or refinancing, with time to act. | Medium |

| Electronics is 78.3% of net sales, and pass-through metals are 40.9% of its sales. | Earnings follow electronics demand and metals prices, so downturns and price swings affect coverage together. | Medium |

| The only covenant located is a springing 5.0 to 1.0 first lien test, with the revolver USD 15.0 million drawn. | The test is far from binding on disclosed figures, but its definitions are not supplied. | Medium |
### Credit view

Element Solutions is a specialty chemicals credit with moderate reported leverage that rose in 2026 and is still serviced comfortably. The strongest support is coverage and liquidity: Adjusted EBITDA of USD 673.1 million over the last twelve months covers cash interest paid of USD 85.7 million 7.85 times, and cash plus undrawn revolver is USD 702.9 million with no maturity before September 2028. The weakest point is the 2026 acquisition year: debt of USD 2,082.1 million is 3.09x LTM Adjusted EBITDA, cash conversion lagged earnings, and earnings depend on electronics demand and metal prices. What decides the outcome is whether earnings growth turns into free cash flow that reduces net leverage of 2.76x before the USD 800.0 million notes mature, and whether shareholder returns stay modest. [CP-1 C4, C5, C7; CP-1A transaction and governance rows]
- Category: Analyst Interpretation, based on CP-1 figures and CP-1A Documentary Fact rows.
- Confidence: Medium. The reported figures reconcile, but covenant definitions, termination terms and pro forma EBITDA are missing, and CP-1A rates this module Ready with limitations.

Thesis: Element Solutions can service its debt from growing earnings with adequate liquidity and a distant first maturity, but 2026 acquisitions lifted leverage, cash conversion is thinner than earnings, and unverified add-backs and covenant terms limit how much comfort the reported ratios give.
### Key findings

1. Leverage rose with the 2026 acquisitions. Total debt rose to USD 2,082.1 million at September 30, 2026 from USD 1,625.9 million at December 31, 2025, while cash fell to USD 224.9 million from USD 626.5 million, so net debt to LTM Adjusted EBITDA is 2.76x against 1.83x at FY2025 (CP-1 C4). Mechanism: EFC was paid from cash and Micromax from USD 450 million of add-on term loans plus revolver borrowings (CP-1A transaction summary), so gross debt rose while the acquired earnings enter LTM only from January 2 and February 2, 2026. Implication: LTM leverage overstates a full-year run rate and is falling as earnings arrive (3.71x at Q1 2026 to 3.09x), but the starting point is higher and the cushion for further debt-funded deals is smaller. Documentary Fact via CP-1; Analyst Interpretation on direction.

2. Coverage is strong. Adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest paid 7.85x and net interest expense 8.29x on the LTM basis (CP-1 C5), slightly below 7.98x on cash interest at FY2025. Mechanism: about 94% of debt is fixed through swaps and the 3.875% USD Notes due 2028, so higher floating rates have limited effect, although the euro-denominated swap legs add currency sensitivity (CP-1 debt register). Implication: low near-term debt service strain unless earnings fall sharply. Documentary Fact via CP-1.

3. Earnings are growing, but part of the growth is acquired or metals-driven. Nine-month 2026 Adjusted EBITDA of USD 536.8 million is above USD 411.3 million a year earlier (CP-1 C13), and quarterly Adjusted EBITDA rose each quarter of 2026. Reported Q3 2026 net sales growth of 52% compares with organic growth of 13% (CP-1), because acquisitions and pass-through metals pricing lifted reported sales (CP-1A operating rows). Mechanism: higher metal prices raise revenue and working capital without proportional profit, and gross margin fell to 34.4% from 42.2% (CP-1A A4). Implication: reported growth overstates underlying growth, and margin should be assessed on an ex-metals basis. Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on quality.

4. Cash conversion lags earnings. Nine-month operating cash flow of USD 192.2 million was 35.8% of Adjusted EBITDA, against 48.3% in the same period of 2025, and below USD 198.7 million a year earlier despite higher earnings (CP-1 C13). Mechanism: receivables and inventories absorbed cash as metal prices rose; Q3 2026 alone produced USD 159.2 million after an outflow of USD 66.6 million in Q1 2026. Implication: free cash flow of USD 182.9 million LTM (CP-1 C6) is thinner than EBITDA suggests and is seasonal and metals-price dependent. Documentary Fact via CP-1.

5. Liquidity is adequate and the first maturity is distant, but larger than liquidity. Cash plus undrawn revolver is USD 702.9 million, of which USD 176 million of cash is held by foreign subsidiaries (CP-1 C7, narrative review). The USD 800.0 million of notes due September 1, 2028 exceed liquidity by USD 97.1 million (CP-1 C13), and term loans of USD 1,279.7 million mature on December 18, 2030. Implication: repayment depends on cash generation or refinancing, with about 22 months to act as at the as-of date; the first maturity is a monitoring point rather than a near-term constraint. Documentary Fact via CP-1.

6. The terminated Solstice merger leaves unanswered questions. A merger signed on July 6, 2026 was terminated on August 27, 2026 with a mutual release, and the Q2 10-Q disclosed a possible USD 376,000,000 termination fee in certain circumstances (CP-1A transaction summary). Whether any fee or cost arose is not stated, and the add-back for acquisition, integration and transaction expenses of USD 52.6 million for nine months 2026 may include process costs (CP-1). Implication: a potential cash cost is unquantified, and the change-of-control risk that would have applied is removed. Documentary Fact for the termination; Insufficient Information for any payment.

7. Shareholder returns and add-backs temper the quality of earnings. Dividends of USD 59.3 million and buybacks of USD 37.7 million in nine months 2026 total USD 97.0 million, with approximately USD 518 million of authorisation remaining (CP-1, CP-1A governance rows); Adjusted EBITDA adds back USD 37.1 million of 2025 executive share grants and USD 52.6 million of acquisition-related costs (CP-1 narrative review). Mechanism: discretionary distributions compete with debt reduction, and add-backs lift the earnings base that leverage ratios use. Implication: leverage tolerance should be read on cash earnings after these items; creditor limits on distributions are not supplied. Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation.

8. Covenant protection is thin on the facts supplied. The only financial covenant located is a springing first lien net leverage test of 5.0 to 1.0, applying when revolver borrowings exceed 30% of the USD 500.0 million commitment; USD 15.0 million is drawn (CP-1). The indicative first lien net leverage is 1.59x and USD 135.0 million of further drawing is possible before the test applies (CP-1 C12), but these are not covenant ratios. Implication: the facility offers little ongoing maintenance discipline while the revolver is lightly used, and headroom cannot be monitored without the Credit Agreement definitions. Documentary Fact; headroom Not calculable.
### Strengths and weaknesses
Strengths:

- Diversified, recurring customer base: no customer is 10% or more of net sales, products are consumed in customers' production, and the business serves electronics, semiconductor, automotive and offshore energy markets (CP-1A operating rows). This supports revenue durability, tempered by minimal order backlog. Documentary Fact.
- Earnings momentum and coverage: Adjusted EBITDA of USD 673.1 million LTM and cash interest cover of 7.85x (CP-1 C1, C5). Documentary Fact via CP-1; Adjusted EBITDA is an issuer non-GAAP measure.

- Liquidity and maturity profile: USD 702.9 million of cash and undrawn revolver, no maturity until the USD 800.0 million notes in September 2028, and about 94% of debt fixed (CP-1 C7, debt register). Documentary Fact via CP-1.

- Financial policy flexibility shown in 2025: USD 200 million of term loans prepaid with divestiture proceeds, and revolver borrowings repaid from USD 85.0 million at Q1 2026 to USD 15.0 million at Q3 2026 (CP-1A governance rows, CP-1). Documentary Fact.
- Reported compliance: the issuer states compliance with the Credit Agreement and indenture covenants at September 30, 2026 (CP-1 covenant table). Management Language; headroom is not verifiable.
Weaknesses:

- Higher leverage after acquisitions: 3.09x total and 2.76x net on LTM Adjusted EBITDA, not pro forma, with tangible stockholders' equity of negative USD 663.4 million after goodwill and intangibles (CP-1 C4, C11). Analyst Interpretation.

- Cash conversion and working capital: operating cash flow was 35.8% of Adjusted EBITDA for nine months 2026, and metals prices drive working capital (CP-1 C13, CP-1A operating rows). Analyst Interpretation.

- Concentration and cyclicality: Electronics is 78.3% of Q3 2026 net sales and 77.6% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, China is 21.9% of FY2025 net sales, and Specialties Adjusted EBITDA fell in Q3 2026 (CP-1A A1, A2). Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation on risk.
- Metals pass-through and margin: pass-through metals are 40.9% of Electronics sales and gross margin fell to 34.4% from 42.2% (CP-1A A3, A4). Documentary Fact.

- Acquisition integration and add-backs: purchase price allocations are preliminary, goodwill of USD 292.7 million was added, and Adjusted EBITDA excludes large acquisition and share-grant items (CP-1A, CP-1). Analyst Interpretation.

- Unverified legal protections: Credit Agreement, indenture and termination terms are not supplied. Insufficient Information; the missing datapoints are covenant definitions, restricted-payment capacity and any payment under the termination, and they matter for headroom and distributions.
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Debt-funded acquisition strategy | Add-on term loans and revolver funded Micromax; further deals could add leverage before earnings catch up | Leverage tolerance narrows; a downturn would raise net leverage quickly | Material |

| Electronics and metals dependence | Electronics is the bulk of sales and profit, and pass-through metals inflate sales and working capital | Earnings, coverage and cash conversion fall together if demand or metal prices turn | Material |
| 2028 notes maturity | USD 800.0 million falls due above current liquidity | Refinancing or cash build is needed; market access risk grows as the date nears | Material |
| Shareholder distributions | Dividends and buybacks are discretionary and creditor limits are not supplied | Cash that could repay debt may leave the group | Minor |
| Quality of Adjusted EBITDA | Large add-backs and non-pro forma LTM make leverage ratios less comparable | Reported leverage may understate or overstate cash earnings | Minor |
| Covenant definitions unknown | A springing 5.0 to 1.0 test applies only above 30% revolver use; definitions not supplied | Headroom cannot be monitored | Minor |
| Terminated merger terms | Possible termination fee or costs not stated | Unquantified cash cost | Minor |
### Gaps
| Gap | Why it matters | Affects | Severity | Action |

| Credit Agreement and indenture not supplied | Covenant headroom, incurrence capacity, restricted payments and change-of-control terms unknown | Covenant risk, governance capacity, key finding 8 | Material | Supply executed documents and add legal review |

| Termination Agreement and any payment not supplied | A possible USD 376,000,000 fee or other cost is unquantified | Key finding 6, liquidity | Material | Supply the August 27, 2026 Form 8-K and exhibit |

| Pro forma EBITDA for EFC and Micromax not supplied | LTM leverage is on a reported basis | Key findings 1 and 2, assessment confidence | Material | Obtain management pro forma or compliance certificate |
| Events after October 22, 2026 not supplied | Position at the as-of date may differ | Monitoring posture | Minor | Supply later filings or confirm none |
| No rating or market data | No external view of the credit | Not required for this scope | Minor | Add only if sourced |
## Calculations

No new calculation. Every figure refers to a CP-1 row or calculation ID (C1 to C13) or a CP-1A calculation (A1 to A7); the 22 months to the 2028 notes is counted from November 5, 2026 to September 1, 2028 and is a date count, not a financial figure.
## Gaps
- Material: the Credit Agreement and indenture, the Termination Agreement and any payment, and pro forma EBITDA for the acquisitions are Not supplied.
- Minor: events after October 22, 2026 are Not supplied; no rating or market data is in scope.
- Restrictions inherited: CP-1A rates this module Ready with limitations, so confidence is Medium rather than High.
## Next module
- CP-5: trace each finding to its CP-1 row or calculation and its CP-1A row, and check that the categories match the basis.
- Report delivery: "Key findings" and "Strengths and weaknesses" above; carry the Medium confidence and the Material gaps.
